To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the two forms of childhood asthma are associated with different airway inflammation patterns.

(1) airways inflammation is present in both atopic and non-atopic asthmatic children, but the type of inflammation differs between these two groups; (2) the non-atopic asthmas are characterized by a neutrophilic inflammatory response that is not associated with increased eosinophilic inflammation; (3) the atopic asthmas have a more typical eosinophilic inflammatory response, but also have a substantial neutrophilic component; (4) both
1) the airways of children with atopy have chronic inflammation and 2) the airways in children with viral-triggered wheezing have no evidence of chronic inflammation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new methods for the diagnosis of asthma and the identification of the underlying causes.
the development, evaluation and application of novel methods for the detection, quantification and characterisation of airborne pollutants and their sources.
understanding the mechanisms of asthma, particularly the role that inflammation plays in the disease process, and the relationship of inflammation to the clinical features of asthma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a strong correlation between asthma and airway inflammation in adults and children.
the presence of airway inflammation in children is a marker for asthma severity and that the presence of eosinophils in the airways is a marker for the atopic type of asthma.
the current evidence does not support the use of inhaled corticosteroids as an effective treatment for children with acute asthma exacerbations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

children with atopic asthma have airways inflammation during both symptomatic and asymptomatic periods, whereas children with non-atopic asthma do not have inflammation during asymptomatic periods, but may have inflammation during symptomatic periods.
the airways in children with asthma are inflamed, but that the nature of this inflammation varies according to the pattern of disease.
there are at least two different phenotypes of asthma, and the one that is associated with the highest levels of airways inflammation is also the one that is most likely to be associated with atopy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
children with atopic asthma, but not those with non-atopic asthma, have persistent airways inflammation during periods of relative symptom stability.
children with atopic asthma have persistent airways inflammation, whereas children with non-atopic asthma have no evidence of persistent airways inflammation.
children with atopic asthma and persistent symptoms have airways inflammation even in the asymptomatic phase.
